svg.title: Separate relative gene order from physical orientation
svg.desc: Given A–B14,B–C6,A–C20 map units, B is between A and C because14+6=20. The two line maps draw A–B–C and C–B–A with intervals proportional to14 and6; they represent the same relative order, not two competing solutions. Physical left-right orientation needs an additional landmark. Wider linked intervals can approach50% recombination like independent loci. An even number of exchanges involving a chromatid can restore parental outer-marker phase, so two-point counts can miss events and underestimate long distances. Sampling, survival and scoring matter; a sample fraction above50% does not justify a reliable two-point map exceeding that ceiling.

g.text: Separate relative gene order from physical orientation
Map distances summarize genetic evidence; they are not a ruler of DNA base pairs.
Given pairwise estimates: A–B = 14, B–C = 6, A–C = 20 cM.
B lies between A and C because 14 + 6 = 20. Reversing the whole map gives the same order.
These distances do not identify which physical chromosome end must be on the left.
Distant loci on one chromosome and loci on different chromosomes can both approach 50%.
An even number of exchanges along a chromatid can restore its outer-marker combination.
Two-point fractions can miss those events; do not turn a near-50% result into a precise long map.
